🥞 Happy Sunday! Smart Brevity™ count: 1,477 words ... 5½ mins. Thanks to Erica Pandey for orchestrating. Edited by Ben Berkowitz.

📱Breaking: President Trump said on Truth Social this morning that, at the request of the military, the proposed 250-foot "triumphal arch" in Washington will house snipers, drones and ammunition for "National Security purposes." Keep reading
 
 
1 big thing: Era of personal agents
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

The long-promised personal AI assistant is finally arriving, with a suddenly crowded field of agents offering to run pieces of your everyday life.

  • Why it matters: For years, tech's "personal assistants" were little more than voice-controlled search boxes. Rapid advances in AI are finally giving them the memory, judgment and autonomy to act on our behalf, Axios chief technology correspondent Ina Fried writes.

Catch up fast: Chatbots answer questions. AI agents can actually do things — shopping, making calls, booking tickets, managing calendars and navigating the web.

  • The model first took off in coding and other professional work. Now it's spilling into the far more intimate terrain of everyday life.

💥 Driving the news: A consumer-agent race has erupted almost overnight, with startups and tech giants pursuing the same basic idea — persistent digital proxies that know your life.

  • Instinct has become buzzy by connecting to users' email, messages, screen, audio and location — then proactively texting or calling to help run their lives. It recently added the ability to make phone calls, and is now in talks for a $10 billion valuation.
  • Grok Bot, launched by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI in August, gives persistent agents their own cloud computers, lets them sign into users' apps and keeps them working around the clock.
  • Meta's Muse brought the concept to a broader consumer audience this month with a polished app, a customizable avatar and deep integration with Meta's ecosystem.
  • Apple's Siri is finally getting its AI overhaul, bringing more context and capability to an assistant already built into hundreds of millions of devices.
  • OpenAI is expected to enter the market soon after hiring the creator of OpenClaw — a breakout hit among AI power users earlier this year — to "drive the next generation of personal agents."

🔭 What we're watching: Becoming someone's default agent could be one of the most valuable relationships in consumer technology.

  • People are likely to share far more with an AI that manages their lives than they did with a search engine.

Read on.
 
 
2. 🦾 Trump plans AI Force
 

Via Truth Social
 

President Trump said he's creating an "AI Force" modeled on the Space Force and will soon name a new AI czar.

  • Why it matters: Trump is doubling down on accelerating AI development with limited regulation, even as the industry's biggest leaders call for stronger safety rules and as public fears grow, Axios' Andrew Pantazi writes.

The latest: Trump offered few details on what this AI Force would actually do, what budget it would have or where it would be placed in the federal government.

  • His Truth Social post said the government would "not in any way hinder or stifle" AI's growth but would look for "BAD" behavior using "our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System."

The intrigue: The AI czar position would revive a role that the White House didn't plan to fill six months ago.

  • David Sacks left the formal AI and crypto czar job in March, though he remains influential as co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.

Read on.
 
 
3. 💰 Trump 2.0's market
 
Data: Financial Modeling Prep. Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals

We're 20 months into President Trump's second term. Axios' Dan Primack reports on how the stock market's performance stacks up against past presidencies:

The market soared during the first 20 months of President Trump's second term, but slightly underperformed the same period of his first term.

  • Why it matters: Trump considers the stock market to be a proxy for the economy, even though many economists disagree, Dan Primack writes.

By the numbers: The S&P 500 rose nearly 27.6% between inauguration day and this past Friday's close, compared to 28.5% during his first term.

  • The gap at 20 months is closer than it was at the one-year mark, with Trump 2.0 leapfrogging former President Biden but still trailing former President Obama.

Zoom in: Trump 2.0 trails Trump 1.0 on the Dow and Nasdaq, but is ahead on the Russell 3000.

Dow Jones Industrial Average:

  • Trump 2.0: 18.8%
  • Biden: 0.3%
  • Trump 1.0: 33.8%
  • Obama: 28.1%

Nasdaq Composite:

  • Trump 2.0: 35.1%
  • Biden: -12.6%
  • Trump 1.0: 43.5%
  • Obama: 51.4%

4. 🎤 Barred reporters move to sidewalk
 
Photos: Jose Luis Magana/AP, Doug Mills/The New York Times

On the left: CNN senior White House reporter Betsy Klein, flashing an empty credential holder, reports across Pennsylvania Avenue from the White House complex yesterday. When she tried to enter, her badge was confiscated under President Trump's "ban" on CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

  • On the right: Akayla Gardner, a White House correspondent for MS NOW, also delivered live hits from across the street after having her badge deactivated.

All three organizations issued statements hinting at legal action. The New York Times, The Washington Post and AP released supportive statements.

  • Go deeper.
 
 
5. 🗞️ Deals eclipse lawsuits
 
Data: Axios research. Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals

Media deals with AI firms have dramatically outpaced lawsuits over the past two years, Kerry Flynn and Sara Fischer report in an Axios Media Trends Executive briefing.

  • Why it matters: The licensing market is developing faster than courts are establishing the underlying rules.

Zoom in: News has moved furthest into the licensing market, although much of that momentum is coming from deals with smaller firms, like ProRata, rather than major companies like Anthropic.

  • Music and book companies have become more litigious over the past two years.

6. 👀 3 GOP power players walk into a bar
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

It sounds like the start of an only-in-D.C. joke, Axios' Marc Caputo reports:

  • Three Republican power players walk into a bar for a freewheeling conversation. They unwittingly sit next to a liberal comic. She then skewers them in an Instagram post recounting their chat.

Why it matters: It became no laughing matter for one of the Republicans — oilman Harry Sargeant — who's trying to improve his uneasy relations with the Trump administration, partly related to his business dealings in Venezuela.

  • His rapprochement efforts were complicated last month when senior administration officials became aware of the comic's social media post, in which she alleged that Sargeant spoke negatively about President Trump.

🥃 Zoom in: The episode unfolded Aug. 18 in the Bourbon Lounge of the Four Seasons hotel in D.C., where comic Suzanne Lambert was working on jokes for an upcoming set, she said in a post to her 495,000 Instagram followers that had 2 million views before she took it down.

  • In the video, Lambert said she coincidentally wound up sitting next to Sargeant and noted a vibe shift when two other men walked in: Pete Marocco and Gentry Beach.
  • Lambert said in her post that she was just "minding my business," but started to pay more attention when the men at the bar began "spouting off about Trump. I hear Trump, Trump, Trump, Trump."
  • At one point, Lambert's post attributed comments to Sargeant that allegedly disparaged Trump and Republicans' midterm chances. Sargeant, through his attorneys, vigorously disputes that.

📱 Behind the scenes: Lambert's video quickly went viral, prompting Sargeant's attorneys to send her a cease and desist letter.

  • Lambert took the post down. But by then, the post had circulated among Trump advisers. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was made aware of it, a source said.
  • "Harry's got some problems, and what the White House saw didn't help," an administration source said of Sargeant.

Keep reading.
 
 
7. 🇨🇳 AI state dinner
 
Photos: AFP via Getty Images

Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in D.C. this week for the first state visit by a Chinese leader in more than a decade:

AI will be a focus of the Trump-Xi summit at the White House on Thursday, and top tech moguls have scored invitations to the hot-ticket state dinner in the East Room.

  • On the guest list, per Axios' Maria Curi and Courtenay Brown: David Sacks, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Apple executive chair Tim Cook, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon, Citi CEO Jane Fraser, Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, plus Michael Dell, Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk.

🛬 When Xi's plane lands at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, Trump will be there to greet him. Trump typically meets foreign leaders at the White House.

  • More on the visit.
 
 
8. 🖼️ 1 for the road: L.A.'s new museum
 
The new 300,000-square-foot Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in L.A.'s Exposition Park. Photo: Mario Tama/Getty Images

"Star Wars" creator George Lucas called his Lucas Museum of Narrative Art a "temple to the people's art." Seventeen years after it was first envisioned, it'll open to the public on Tuesday in Los Angeles.

  • The museum mixes popular and commercial art with fine art, drawn largely from the collections of Lucas and his wife and co-founder, businesswoman Mellody Hobson.

What you'll see:

  • 💫 The "Star Wars in Motion" exhibit shows vehicles used in the original trilogy and the Lucas-directed prequels. The outdoor paths feature statues of Carrie Fisher's Princess Leia, Natalie Portman's Padmé Amidala, Yoda and Grogu.
  • 🎨 There are paintings by Norman Rockwell and Frida Kahlo and murals by Banksy and Diego Rivera.
  • 🐶 "Poker Game," Cassius Marcellus Coolidge's kitschy 1894 painting of a group of dogs playing cards, hangs steps from a Kahlo self-portrait — a perfect merger of high and low art.
